about.title: La Puente Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Falls happen fast, but the aftermath in La Puente can drag on for weeks — medical visits, missed shifts, and calls from the property's insurer asking for a statement. Whether the incident happened in a shopping plaza off Valley Boulevard, an apartment stairwell near Amar Road, or a business along Temple Avenue, California law asks a specific question: did the property owner know, or should they have known, about the hazard in time to fix it or warn you? That's the heart of a premises liability case here. LawProactive doesn't practice law — we're a free service that connects people hurt on someone else's property with an independent attorney who can evaluate what happened, gather the evidence that matters, and explain your options. There's no fee unless the attorney recovers something for you, and reaching out costs nothing.

whyChoose.title: Why the Notice Requirement Matters in La Puente Cases

items.title: Proving the Owner Knew or Should Have Known
items.desc: California law generally requires showing the property owner had notice of the hazard and failed to address it. An attorney can help identify maintenance logs, prior complaints, or repeat incidents that establish that knowledge.

items.title: Surveillance Video Disappears Fast
items.desc: Many La Puente businesses and apartment complexes overwrite security footage within days or weeks. Acting quickly to request preservation of that video can be the difference between having proof and having none.

items.title: Comparative Fault Can Reduce, Not Erase, a Claim
items.desc: Even if you were partly distracted or moving quickly when you fell, California's pure comparative fault rule means you may still recover something — your share of fault simply reduces the amount, it doesn't bar the claim.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in La Puente?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit against a private property owner. If the fall happened on public property, such as a sidewalk maintained by the city or county, the deadline is much shorter and involves an earlier claim-filing step. Because these timelines vary, it's worth having an attorney review the details of your specific fall soon.

items.question: What if I fell at a store or apartment complex and there's no video?
items.answer: Video isn't required to bring a claim, though it helps. Photos of the hazard, incident reports, witness names, and even weather or lighting conditions at the time can all support your case. An attorney can also send a formal request asking the property to preserve any existing footage before it's deleted.

items.question: Does it matter that this happened in La Puente specifically?
items.answer: Local details can matter — for example, whether the hazard was on a well-traveled corridor like Hacienda Boulevard or Amar Road, or inside a private business, changes who is responsible and what evidence is available. An attorney familiar with claims in this part of Los Angeles County can factor in those specifics when evaluating your situation.

items.question: Will I have to pay anything upfront to talk to an attorney?
items.answer: No. LawProactive's connection service is free, and attorneys in the network typically work on contingency, meaning there's no fee unless they recover compensation for you. There's no obligation to move forward after speaking with an attorney.
